fetched_contents.text: Chromoblastomycosis Key Facts * Chromoblastomycosis is an infection under the skin caused by fungi. * It occurs sporadically in tropical and subtropical climates, and its global incidence is unknown. * The infection can be disfiguring, causing wart-like lesions of the skin which spread slowly to adjacent areas. It causes disfigurement and disability, and in rare cases skin cancer. * Chromoblastomycosis is diagnosed with laboratory tools such as microscopy and culture. More accurate molecular diagnostic methods are in development. * Safe and effective antifungal medicines are available for treatment. ---------------------------------------- Overview Chromoblastomycosis is a sporadically occurring infection seen in tropical and subtropical climates caused by a number of different pigmented fungi, the most common of which are Fonsecaea pedrosoi, Fonsecaea monophora and Cladophialophora carrionii. Other fungi can also cause chromoblastomycosis. Chromoblastomycosis can cause disability due to limb enlargement, which may lead to inability to work and considerable social stigma. Rarely, the fungi that cause chromoblastomycosis can infect other organs, such as the brain, or lead to skin cancer. Who is at risk? Chromoblastomycosis affects normal healthy people and is mainly seen in adults. Agricultural workers are the most common occupational group to be infected. Signs and symptoms Chromoblastomycosis presents with wart-like lesions on exposed areas of the skin such as the legs or forearms. These can exceed 10 centimetres in diameter. Patches of skin may also appear flattened (plaque-like) and show central scarring or atrophy, but they are not itchy or painful. Pain and itching can appear in moderate or severe disease. Small dark spots can be seen on the surface of lesions and represent clusters of the pigmented fungal cells – an important diagnostic clue. Large lesions cause severe limb swelling and discomfort, limiting movement. In longstanding cases, secondary bacterial infections are common and the smell from affected limbs may be unpleasant, which may also lead to social exclusion. There is a risk of development of squamous cell carcinoma of the skin in longstanding untreated lesions. Although the infection usually remains in one body region, local spread through the lymphatics, and very rarely blood stream dissemination to the central nervous system, can occur. Transmission This infection occurs when fungi from the natural environment invade deeper parts of an individual’s skin after their skin is damaged by a superficial abrasion or a penetrating injury. An infected person cannot directly transmit the infection to other people. Intermediate vectors, such as mosquitoes, do not transmit chromoblastomycosis. Treatment Chromoblastomycosis can be treated with oral itraconazole or terbinafine. Voriconazole, intravenous amphotericin B and oral flucytosine have also been used. Other methods of treatment include local application of heat, cryotherapy and photodynamic therapy. Surgical reductions have been used but should be given following initial chemotherapy to avoid local recurrence. Early treatment is key, providing the best results after about 3–6 months. Patients with large or extensive chromoblastomycosis and limb swelling often require over a year of treatment and there may be residual lymphoedema in such cases. There is no evidence that different fungal species respond differently to the antifungal medicines recommended for treatment. Challenges The earliest lesions of chromoblastomycosis are small, raised lumps or nodules on the skin surface with no specific visible diagnostic features. Therefore, diagnosis depends on demonstrating the characteristic thick-walled, single or multicellular clusters of pigmented fungal cells, known as muriform or sclerotic bodies, either in scrapings from lesions or in histopathology of biopsy material. Clusters of these cells can be found in the dark spots seen on the surface of the skin lesions and these provide the best sites for taking a skin scraping with a scalpel blade or for a biopsy. Culture or molecular diagnosis is helpful in confirming the diagnosis but decisions on treatment can be made without identification of the organism. All laboratory diagnostic methods require specialized skills and training, and there is currently insufficient diagnostic expertise in many endemic areas. The cost of effective antifungal medicines in endemic countries is a major challenge that can limit successful completion of treatment as patients often cannot afford them. Global impact The largest number of cases of chromoblastomycosis has occurred in Central America and northern South America, Africa, China and the West Pacific. Brazil, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Madagascar and Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of) have reported the most cases. The global incidence of chromoblastomycosis is unknown. WHO response Chromoblastomycosis is recognized as a neglected tropical disease (NTD) and is included in the NTD road map 2021−2030 to increase surveillance and visibility of the disease. In 2022, WHO published the skin NTD framework to promote integration across different skin diseases and support the evolving Programme for Skin NTDs. One of the key challenges of chromoblastomycosis is the lack of information on its global prevalence as cases are not currently reported. Skin NTD programmes are expected to provide more data on incidence of the infection. The 2021−2030 roadmap promotes early identification of affected individuals. This can be achieved through training of health care workers aimed at improving awareness and disease recognition. Capacity strengthening on skin NTDs is key. Chromoblastomycosis is included in several WHO technical resources such as the Skin NTD training manual and mobile app as well as a dedicated online course available on the OpenWHO platform: Chromoblastomycosis: training for national and district-level health workers.

fetched_contents.text: Clinical Overview of Chromoblastomycosis | Chromoblastomycosis * Chromoblastomycosis is an implantation fungal infection caused by melanized, dematiaceous fungi that live in soil and on wood and plants. * It most often occurs in tropical and subtropical regions, but cases have been reported in the United States. * Lesions may resemble other infectious or non-infectious skin lesions. * Without treatment, chromoblastomycosis can cause limb swelling, difficulty walking, skin cancer, and scarring of the skin. * These physical effects can lead to social stigma. Etiology Chromoblastomycosis occurs when a break in the skin allows fungi to enter. It is caused by melanized, dematiaceous (black) fungi. Reservoir and endemic areas These fungi are associated with certain plants (e.g., thorns of Mimosa plant, Madagascar palm house plant, babassu coconut). Some species are more common in certain climates. For example, F. pedrosoi and F. nubica infections are commonly acquired in tropical regions, while C. carrionii infections are more commonly acquired in semiarid regions. Types The most common causes of chromoblastomycosis are Fonsecaea pedrosoi, F. monophora, F. nubica, Cladophialophora carrionii, Rhinocladiella aquaspersa, and Phialophora verrucosa. However, species distribution varies by region and climatic conditions. Resource Take the self-paced free online course on Neglected Fungal Tropical Diseases: Chromoblastomycosis, Sporotrichosis, and Mycetoma. Learn best practices in recognition, diagnosis, and management of these often-overlooked diseases and earn continuing education credit. Risk factors Clinical consult Healthcare providers can call 404-639-5168 or email fungalconsult@cdc.gov for consultation on diagnosis or treatment for suspected or confirmed fungal diseases. Chromoblastomycosis can affect immunocompetent and immunocompromised individuals including people who are malnourished. It is more common in people who work or perform activities outdoors (e.g., farmers, gardeners, forestry workers, vendors of farm products). Lack of protective gear (e.g. shoes, gloves), poor hygiene, and inadequate nutrition may increase the chance of getting chromoblastomycosis. Clinical features Chromoblastomycosis is a chronic progressive fungal infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue. Most infections present on the lower or upper limbs, but infections can occur anywhere on the body. Typically, the infection first presents as erythematous papules (sometimes macules) at the site of inoculation. Over time, these lesions may progress covering larger areas of the skin with nodular, verrucous, tumoral, plaque, or scar-like morphologies. Chromoblastomycosis progresses slowly over months to years. If left untreated can cause lymphedema, secondary bacterial infections, squamous cell carcinoma, tissue fibrosis, difficulty walking, and social stigma. Prevention Using personal protective equipment (e.g., gloves, shoes, appropriate clothing) and water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) may help prevent infections. There are no available vaccines for chromoblastomycosis. Early diagnosis and treatment can prevent severe disease, disability, and long-term complications. Diagnosis Diagnosis starts with obtaining skin scrapings from lesions or a skin biopsy. Confirming chromoblastomycosis depends on visualizing microscopically the characteristic thick-walled, single, or multicellular clusters of pigmented fungal cells. These fungal cells, often with pigmented internal cross walls, resemble copper pennies. These are also known as 'medlar bodies', 'muriform cells', or 'sclerotic bodies.' Clusters of these cells can be found in the dark spots seen on the surface of the skin lesions. These provide the best sites for taking a skin scraping with a scalpel blade or for a biopsy. Microscopy: Examination of skin scrapings through direct microscopy with a potassium hydroxide (KOH) mount can identify these characteristic pigmented fungal cells. Histopathology: Examination of a skin biopsy can find the presence of pigmented fungal cells in the dermis. Culture and molecular diagnosis: Helpful in confirming the diagnosis. Decisions on treatment can be made without identification of the organism. Fungi that cause chromoblastomycosis are slow-growing and can take weeks before growing by culture. There are no commercially available serologic tests available. Treatment and recovery Global guidelines are not available for treatment of chromoblastomycosis. Prolonged oral therapy (months to years) is often required. Itraconazole is typically considered first-line therapy with cure rates ranging from 15–80%. Terbinafine is also frequently used to treat chromoblastomycosis. It may offer advantages over itraconazole such as better absorption and fewer drug-drug interactions. Other triazole agents such as voriconazole and posaconazole have been reported to have favorable clinical response in refractory disease. Combination therapy with itraconazole and terbinafine or 5-flucytosine have been used in clinical practice for severe or refractory disease. There is no evidence that different fungal species respond differently to the antifungal medicines recommended for treatment. Other methods of treatment include topical immune response modulators, local application of heat, cryotherapy, and photodynamic therapy. Treatment Access Over 78 million people globally may not have access to itraconazole. Clinicians may resort to using ketoconazole, an antifungal drug less effective and associated with severe hepatotoxicity risk. Surveillance and Statistics Chromoblastomycosis is designated as a neglected tropical disease by the World Health Organization. Chromoblastomycosis is not reportable in any U.S. jurisdiction or in most countries globally. Reliable disease burden estimates are lacking due to absence of national, regional, or global disease surveillance systems or networks. fetched_contents.text: Chromoblastomycosis is curable with DAT therapy (debulking, intralesional amphotericin B, oral terbinafine); case series of 16 patients Abstract Once incurable and chronic devastating diseases of chromomycosis is now curable with, debulking, intralesional amphotericin B and oral terbinafine (DAT). Debulking methods ranged from electrocautery to total surgical excision according to the size and the site of the lesion; a diluted solution of 1 mg/mL of amphotericin B (AMB) was injected weekly at the edge of the lesion; and simultaneous treatment with daily 500 mg oral terbinafine. Voriconazole 200 mg twice daily was added in one patient who had infection spread along the right lower limb for more than 20 years. DAT therapy was continued until complete clinical clearance where 14 out of 16 (87.5%) were cured using intralesional AMB 4–8 weeks (mean 5.8, mode 7) and oral terbinafine 6–12 weeks (mean 9.6, mode 12). Two patients who had lesions for 10 years and 20 years had to continue treatments for 14 weeks and 34 weeks, respectively, leaving scarring, chronic lymphedema, or depigmentation to a lesser degree. Early initiation of treatment gives an optimal outcome in a shorter period of time without residual sequelae. It is caused by traumatic inoculation and is commonly found in farmers, manual labourers, and barefoot walkers. Its recalcitrant and polymorphic nature makes its diagnosis and management difficult. In this case series, we report 16 patients whom were successfully cured in two centers in Sri Lanka during 1-year period from 2022 to 2023. Methods These 16 patients, 14 men and 2 women, were diagnosed clinically and were confirmed histopathologically many years back and were on the various treatment modalities for 6 months–20-year duration distressing both patients and the physicians. Recent advances and treatment outcomes for chromoblastomycosis suggest that combination therapy and newer delivery strategies are gaining attention, but the evidence remains mostly observational and case-based rather than large randomized trials.

New drugs, combinations, or delivery strategies: The most notable recent advance in the evidence is combination therapy, particularly itraconazole plus terbinafine. One case report described a patient cured by combined injection of glucan and oral itraconazole [N4-R1], while another reported excellent preliminary results from daily itraconazole 400 mg plus terbinafine 250 mg [N4-R2]. A case series from Sri Lanka reported DAT therapy (debulking, intralesional amphotericin B, oral terbinafine) as curable, with intralesional amphotericin B administered weekly and oral terbinafine daily [N2-F3]. Another case series noted that combination therapy was effective in four patients with poorly responsive chromoblastomycosis, with some success using alternative week treatment [N3-R3]. A separate case also described cryotherapy combined with oral terbinafine for 6 months achieving cure with minimal local adverse effects [N4-R5]. These examples point to a trend toward combination regimens, adjunctive local therapies, and intralesional antifungal delivery, but they are not large-scale studies.

Reported cure rates and treatment failure patterns: The Sri Lanka DAT case series reported 14 out of 16 patients (87.5%) cured, with treatment durations varying from 6 weeks to 34 weeks [N2-F3]. This is the strongest reported cure rate in the provided evidence. The WHO and CDC sources describe prolonged oral therapy as often required, with cure rates ranging from 15–80% for itraconazole [N1-F2]. They also note that refractory disease may require voriconazole, intravenous amphotericin B, or 5-flucytosine [N1-F2]. The evidence does not provide a single consensus cure rate for Africa specifically, but it does suggest variability: some patients may respond well to first-line antifungals, while others need combination therapy or more aggressive intervention. The CDC also emphasizes that treatment failure patterns are not clearly described in the evidence provided, and that long-term outcomes remain an important concern [N1-F2].

Long-term outcomes and relapse data: The Sri Lanka case series reported follow-up after treatment completion and observed no side effects to drugs, with patients reviewed monthly for 3 months and then every 3–6 months for 1 year to observe recurrence [N2-F3]. This suggests that relapse monitoring is part of modern practice, but the evidence does not give a relapse rate. The CDC notes that treatment can take 3–6 months and may require over a year for large or extensive disease, with possible residual lymphedema [N1-F2]. It also warns that longstanding untreated lesions can progress to squamous cell carcinoma, and that early treatment is key to preventing severe disease and long-term complications [N1-F2]. The evidence therefore supports a cautious view: long-term outcomes are generally better with early treatment, but relapse and residual disability can still occur, especially in extensive or poorly responsive cases.

Overall, the recent advances in chromoblastomycosis treatment are best summarized as a shift toward combination antifungal regimens, adjunctive local therapies, and more aggressive local interventions like intralesional amphotericin B. Cure rates appear to vary considerably, with the highest reported success in the DAT case series, while long-term outcomes remain dependent on early and sustained treatment and close follow-up [N2-F3][N1-F2].

## 2) Treatment options and local implementation in Africa

Treatment in Africa is typically guided by first-line and second-line antifungal drugs, with surgery used for refractory or localized disease. The evidence also shows that implementation barriers such as cost, drug availability, and adherence are major concerns.

### First-line and second-line antifungal drugs used
The WHO and CDC both list **oral itraconazole** and **terbinafine** as the main first-line treatments [N1-F2]. The CDC also notes that **voriconazole, intravenous amphotericin B, and oral flucytosine** have been used, with **voriconazole** and **posaconazole** reported as favorable for refractory disease [N1-F2]. In the Sri Lanka DAT case series, treatment included **intralesional amphotericin B** plus **oral terbinafine**, and one patient also received **voriconazole** [N2-F3]. This suggests a tiered approach: itraconazole and terbinafine as first-line, and intravenous amphotericin B, voriconazole, posaconazole, or 5-flucytosine as second-line or adjunctive options for severe or refractory disease [N1-F2][N2-F3].

### Surgical indications and when surgery is combined with drugs
Surgery is indicated for **localized disease** or **lesions refractory to antifungal therapy** [N3-R1]. The ESCMID/ECMM guidelines state that excision alone is rarely sufficient and that surgery should be combined with prolonged systemic antifungal therapy [N3-R2]. The Sri Lanka case series used **debulking, intralesional amphotericin B, and oral terbinafine**, with debulking methods including electrocautery, curettage, and surgical excision depending on lesion size and site [N2-F3]. Another case report described **surgical excision with skin grafting** followed by antifungal therapy [N3-R3]. These examples show that surgery is typically used in **combination with antifungal drugs** rather than as standalone treatment [N3-R2][N2-F3].

### Barriers to treatment access and adherence
The evidence points to several implementation barriers:
- Access to effective antifungal medicines is a major challenge in endemic countries, with patients often unable to afford treatment [N1-F2].
- Over 78 million people globally may not have access to itraconazole [N1-F2].
- Delayed diagnosis and inadequate therapy are problems in Africa [N6-R1].
- The WHO and CDC describe the need for specialized laboratory skills and training, which are lacking in many endemic areas [N1-F2].
- General literature on fungal diseases in Africa highlights delayed diagnosis, inadequate therapy, and implementation challenges [N6-R1].
- The CDC notes that early diagnosis and treatment can prevent severe disease, disability, and long-term complications, but that this is difficult when access is limited [N1-F2].

In conclusion, treatment in Africa is usually **first-line itraconazole and terbinafine**, with **surgery and second-line antifungals** used for refractory or extensive disease [N1-F2][N2-F3]. Surgery is combined with prolonged antifungal therapy rather than used alone [N3-R2]. Implementation barriers include limited access to affordable medicines, weak diagnostic capacity, and poor adherence, all of which are compounded by the chronic nature of the disease and the need for long-term follow-up [N1-F2][N6-R1].

## 3) Recent advances and treatment outcomes

Recent advances suggest a growing emphasis on **combination therapy**, **adjunctive local therapies**, and **more aggressive local interventions**, but the evidence remains mostly observational and case-based rather than large randomized trials.

### New drugs, combinations, or delivery strategies
The most notable recent advance is **combination therapy**. One case report described a patient cured by combined injection of glucan and oral itraconazole [N4-R1]. Another reported excellent preliminary results from daily itraconazole 400 mg plus terbinafine 250 mg [N4-R2]. A case series from Sri Lanka reported **DAT therapy** (debulking, intralesional amphotericin B, oral terbinafine) as curable, with intralesional amphotericin B administered weekly and oral terbinafine daily [N2-F3]. Another case series noted that combination therapy was effective in four patients with poorly responsive chromoblastomycosis, with some success using alternative week treatment [N3-R3]. A separate case also described **cryotherapy combined with oral terbinafine** for 6 months achieving cure with minimal local adverse effects [N4-R5]. These examples point to a trend toward combination regimens, adjunctive local therapies, and intralesional antifungal delivery, but they are not large-scale studies.

### Reported cure rates and treatment failure patterns
The Sri Lanka DAT case series reported **14 out of 16 patients (87.5%) cured**, with treatment durations varying from 6 weeks to 34 weeks [N2-F3]. This is the strongest reported cure rate in the provided evidence. The WHO and CDC describe prolonged oral therapy as often required, with cure rates ranging from **15–80% for itraconazole** [N1-F2]. They also note that refractory disease may require **voriconazole, intravenous amphotericin B, or 5-flucytosine** [N1-F2]. The evidence does not provide a single consensus cure rate for Africa specifically, but it does suggest variability: some patients may respond well to first-line antifungals, while others need combination therapy or more aggressive intervention. The CDC also emphasizes that treatment failure patterns are not clearly described in the evidence provided, and that long-term outcomes remain an important concern [N1-F2].

### Long-term outcomes and relapse data
The Sri Lanka case series reported follow-up after treatment completion and observed no side effects to drugs, with patients reviewed monthly for 3 months and then every 3–6 months for 1 year to observe recurrence [N2-F3]. This suggests that relapse monitoring is part of modern practice, but the evidence does not give a relapse rate. The CDC notes that treatment can take **3–6 months** and may require **over a year** for large or extensive disease, with possible residual lymphedema [N1-F2]. It also warns that longstanding untreated lesions can progress to squamous cell carcinoma, and that early treatment is key to preventing severe disease and long-term complications [N1-F2]. The evidence therefore supports a cautious view: long-term outcomes are generally better with early and sustained treatment and close follow-up, but relapse and residual disability can still occur, especially in extensive or poorly responsive cases [N2-F3][N1-F2].

## 4) Africa-specific epidemiology, endemic regions, and disease burden

Africa-specific epidemiology and burden indicate that chromoblastomycosis is a major problem in the region, but reliable burden estimates remain scarce.

### Which African regions are most affected
The WHO fact sheet states that the largest number of cases have occurred in Central America and northern South America, Africa, China, and the West Pacific, with Brazil, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Madagascar, and Venezuela reporting the most cases [N1-F2]. The global disease burden observation in the search results also notes that prevalence varies by region, with certain areas reporting higher numbers [N5-R2]. While the evidence does not list a precise map of African endemic regions, it does imply that chromoblastomycosis is common in tropical and subtropical Africa, with a focus on rural and occupational settings where farmers, gardeners, and manual laborers are at risk [N1-F2]. The WHO also notes that the infection is more common in people who work outdoors and that protective gear, poor hygiene, and inadequate nutrition increase risk [N1-F2]. This suggests that endemic regions in Africa are likely to be rural agricultural areas and places with occupational exposure to soil and plant material.

### Prevalence, incidence, and reporting gaps
The evidence is very thin on precise African prevalence and incidence numbers. The WHO states that the global incidence is unknown and that chromoblastomycosis is not reportable in most countries globally [N1-F2]. The global burden review also says that local epidemiological studies are needed because the global incidence remains unclear [N5-R1]. The CDC similarly notes that reliable disease burden estimates are lacking due to absence of national, regional, or global disease surveillance systems [N1-F2]. In Africa, the burden is therefore likely underestimated because of poor reporting, weak surveillance, and lack of standardized case ascertainment. The evidence does not provide a specific African prevalence figure, so any claim about prevalence would be speculative based on the provided material [N5-R1][N1-F2].

### Burden on health systems and patient populations
The disease burden on health systems is considerable because chromoblastomycosis is a neglected tropical disease and is included in the WHO NTD roadmap [N1-F2]. The WHO notes that there is no evidence that different fungal species respond differently to recommended antifungals, but that prolonged oral therapy is often required and that over 78 million people globally may not have access to itraconazole [N1-F2]. The CDC states that treatment can take **3–6 months** and may require **over a year** for large or extensive disease, with possible residual lymphedema [N1-F2]. It also notes that the infection can cause **limb swelling, difficulty walking, skin cancer, and scarring**, which can lead to **social stigma** [N1-F2]. These effects imply that chromoblastomycosis places a heavy burden on patients, especially those in low-resource settings, and on health systems that must provide long-term antifungal treatment, surgery, and follow-up.

In short, the evidence indicates that chromoblastomycosis is endemic in tropical and subtropical Africa, particularly among rural agricultural workers, but precise prevalence and incidence data are sparse and unreliable [N1-F2][N5-R1]. The disease burden on health systems is significant because of the need for prolonged treatment, the lack of reporting, and the social and physical sequelae described in the sources [N1-F2].

## 5) Bottom line

### Diagnosis
In Africa, chromoblastomycosis is diagnosed most commonly by **microscopy and histopathology**, with **culture** used selectively and **serology** absent from the evidence provided [N1-F2].

### Treatment
First-line treatment is **itraconazole** and **terbinafine**, with **surgery** used for refractory or localized disease and combined with prolonged antifungal therapy [N1-F2][N3-R2]. Second-line options include **intravenous amphotericin B, voriconazole, posaconazole, and 5-flucytosine** for severe or refractory disease [N1-F2][N2-F3]. Implementation barriers include limited access to affordable medicines, weak diagnostic capacity, and poor adherence [N1-F2][N6-R1].

### Recent advances
Recent advances emphasize **combination therapy**, **adjunctive local therapies**, and **intralesional antifungal delivery**, such as **DAT therapy** (debulking, intralesional amphotericin B, oral terbinafine) [N2-F3]. The strongest reported cure rate in the evidence is **87.5%** in a Sri Lanka case series, but the evidence remains observational and case-based [N2-F3][N1-F2].

### Outcomes
Long-term outcomes are generally better with early and sustained treatment and close follow-up, but relapse and residual disability can still occur, especially in extensive or poorly responsive cases [N2-F3][N1-F2].

### Epidemiology
Africa-specific epidemiology suggests that chromoblastomycosis is common in rural tropical and subtropical settings, but precise prevalence and incidence data are sparse and unreliable [N1-F2][N5-R1]. The burden on health systems and patients is considerable because of the chronic nature of the disease, the need for long-term treatment, and the social and physical sequelae described in the sources [N1-F2].

Overall, chromoblastomycosis in Africa remains a challenging, neglected, but treatable disease. The key to improving outcomes is strengthening diagnosis, expanding access to affordable antifungals, improving adherence, and using combination and adjunctive strategies where appropriate [N1-F2][N2-F3][N6-R1].
